sources.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
sources.excerpt: Sunlight reaches Earth's atmosphere and is scattered in all directions by all the gases and particles in the air. Blue light is scattered more than the other colors because it travels as shorter, smaller waves. Closer to the horizon, the sky fades to a lighter blue or white. The sunlight reaching us from low in the sky has passed through even more air than the sunlight reaching us from overhead. As the Sun gets lower in the sky, its light is passing through more of the atmosphere to reach you. Even more of the blue light is scattered, allowing the reds and yellows to pass straight through to your eyes. The sky appears red because small particles of dust, pollution, or other aerosols also scatter blue light, leaving more purely red and yellow light to go through the air.

sources.excerpt: Relative Rayleigh scattering strength scales with 1/wavelength^4, normalised to red at 675 nm: violet 400 nm 8.11, blue 450 nm 5.06, green 530 nm 2.63, yellow 580 nm 1.83, orange 620 nm 1.40, red 675 nm 1.00. Path through a flat atmosphere is 1/sin(elevation): sun overhead 1.00, 60 degrees 1.15, 45 degrees 1.41, 30 degrees 2.00, 20 degrees 2.92, 15 degrees 3.86, 10 degrees 5.76, 5 degrees 11.47. sources.title: Color Blindness
sources.excerpt: at causes color vision deficiency? Most people who have color vision deficiency are born with it. This is because the most common types of color vision deficiency are genetic, meaning they’re passed down from parents. Color vision deficiency can also happen because of an injury to the retina (the light-sensitive layer of tissue in the back of the eye), the optic nerve (which connects the eye to the brain), or the brain itself. Some examples of injuries that can lead to color vision deficiency are: Retinal detachment (when the retina is pulled away from its normal position at the back of the eye) Eye injuries caused by lasers Some kinds of brain tumors — especially ones that affect the optic nerve or put pressure on the brain Radiation treatments Color vision may also get worse as you get older — often because of cataracts (cloudy areas in the lens of the eye). Learn more about what causes color vision deficiency Did you know? Everyone sees color a little differently — including people who don’t have color vision deficiency About 1 in 12 men have color vision deficiency Most people with color vision deficiency are born with it, but sometimes it doesn’t show up until later in life How can I find out if I have color deficiency? During the most common type of test, your eye doctor will show you a circle made of many different colored dots. chapters.heading: Why sunlight splits into different colors
chapters.summary: Explains that sunlight is scattered by air molecules and that shorter blue waves scatter more strongly than longer red waves, with measured Rayleigh ratios showing violet scatters far more than red.

utterances.spokenText: Sunlight reaching Earth is scattered in all directions by gases and particles in the atmosphere. The light does not travel straight through to your eyes completely unchanged.
Every color in the sunlight gets redirected by the air as it passes through the sky. This scattering happens constantly all around you during the day.
Blue light is scattered more than other colors because it travels as shorter, smaller waves. Those very short waves bounce off air molecules more often.
Because shorter wavelengths redirect more easily, blue light spreads across the sky. It really reaches your eyes from every direction instead of straight from the Sun.
utterances.captionText: Short waves spread across the sky

utterances.spokenText: Rayleigh scattering strength scales with one over wavelength to the fourth power. We set red light at six hundred seventy five nanometres as the reference, so its relative strength is exactly one.
utterances.captionText: Inverse fourth power law, red at 675 nm is baseline.

utterances.spokenText: Since violet light travels at about four hundred nanometres, its much shorter wavelength means it gets scattered far more aggressively than longer red waves.
utterances.captionText: Shorter violet waves scatter much more than red.

utterances.spokenText: That is a huge difference: short violet waves are redirected roughly eight times more efficiently than long red waves, which is why the effect is so lopsided.
utterances.captionText: Violet is redirected about eight times more than red.

utterances.spokenText: Green at 530 nanometers scatters 2.63 times as strongly as red at 675 nanometers. Yellow at 580 nanometers scatters 1.83 times as strongly as red.
utterances.captionText: Green scatters 2.63× more than red; yellow scatters 1.83× more.

chapters.heading: How the sky changes from blue overhead to red at the horizon
chapters.summary: Compares the air mass sunlight travels through at different solar elevations and shows how increasing path length removes more blue light, leaving reds and yellows near sunset.

utterances.spokenText: When the Sun sits directly overhead, its light passes through exactly one unit of atmosphere. But at thirty degrees elevation, that same sunlight travels through about two full units of air.
Near the horizon, at just five degrees elevation, sunlight must cross roughly eleven point four seven units of atmosphere before it finally reaches your eyes.
utterances.captionText: At 5 degrees: about 11.47 units of air.

utterances.spokenText: Because that sunlight has passed through so much extra air, the sky closer to the horizon fades to a lighter blue or even white.
utterances.captionText: Horizon sky fades to lighter blue or white.

utterances.spokenText: This happens because low-angle sunlight travels through much more atmosphere than light coming from straight overhead, scattering away more blue along the way.
utterances.captionText: Low-angle light crosses much more air.

utterances.spokenText: As the Sun sinks lower, its light cuts through a thicker slice of sky. More blue gets scattered away before it reaches you, so the reds and yellows pass straight through to your eyes.
utterances.captionText: Low-angle light leaves reds and yellows

utterances.spokenText: Overhead, sunlight crosses just one layer of air. Near the horizon it crosses many layers, so almost all the blue is stripped out before the light arrives.
utterances.captionText: More air strips out the blue

utterances.spokenText: Dust, smoke, and pollution add even more scattering. These tiny particles boost the reddening effect, which is why hazy sunsets can look especially deep red.
Clean air after rain can still turn red, but dirty air makes the effect stronger. Either way, particles help paint the evening sky.
Color vision deficiency means a person sees colors differently than most people. Most of the time, it makes it hard to tell the difference between certain colors.
utterances.captionText: Color vision deficiency changes how colors appear.

chapters.heading: The main ways people see color differently
chapters.summary: Defines color vision deficiency, lists the common red-green and blue-yellow types, notes rare complete deficiency, and states that most affected people manage everyday activities.

utterances.spokenText: The most common type of color vision deficiency makes red and green hard to distinguish. People with it often confuse these two colors in daily life, at work, and outdoors.
utterances.captionText: Red-green is the most common type

props.title: Red-Green Deficiency
steps: Hard to distinguish red and green

utterances.spokenText: Red-green deficiency is the most common form of color vision deficiency. People with it struggle to tell red from green in many situations.
Another type makes blue and yellow look the same. These colors can appear nearly identical to people with this deficiency, especially in dim light.
utterances.captionText: Blue-yellow looks the same to some

utterances.spokenText: Blue-yellow deficiency is much less common than the red-green type. It can make certain shades of blue and yellow nearly impossible to separate.
In rare cases, a person has complete color vision deficiency. They may see almost no color at all, rather than just struggling to separate one pair of similar hues.
utterances.captionText: Complete color vision deficiency is rare

utterances.spokenText: Even so, seeing nothing but gray and white is rare. That total loss comes with complete deficiency, which is itself the uncommon case.
utterances.captionText: Complete loss is the rare case

utterances.spokenText: Most people with color vision deficiency are born with it. The common types are genetic, meaning they are passed down from parents through their families.
utterances.captionText: Most color vision deficiency is inherited

utterances.spokenText: Because it runs in families, the trait often appears across generations. It is usually present from early childhood and lasts throughout a person's life.
Not every case is inherited. Color vision deficiency can also result from an injury to the retina, the optic nerve, or the brain itself, appearing later in life.
utterances.captionText: Injury can cause color vision deficiency.

utterances.spokenText: Specific injuries can lead to color vision deficiency. Examples include retinal detachment, laser eye injuries, and certain brain tumors affecting the optic nerve in adults.
utterances.captionText: Retinal detachment, laser injuries, optic nerve tumors.

chapters.heading: Why color vision differences happen: genes and injury
chapters.summary: Explains that most color vision deficiency is inherited and genetic, while acquired forms can result from retinal, optic nerve, or brain injuries such as detachment, laser damage, or tumors.

utterances.spokenText: Color vision deficiency usually runs in families, passed from parents to children through inherited genes. Most people who have it are born with the condition.
Because the trait is genetic, it often appears across several generations of the same family. Parents pass it on, and it is usually there from early childhood.
The pattern follows family lines. Men are affected far more often than women, which is why the condition looks so uneven across the population.
The inherited form is present from birth and usually remains stable throughout life. Because it runs in families, relatives often share the same type of color vision difference.
Color vision differences are often present from birth, but there is no cure for the condition. Most people simply learn to adapt to the way they see the world every day.
Special glasses and tinted contact lenses can help some people tell colors apart more easily. These aids improve contrast, though they do not restore typical color vision completely.
When an injury to the retina, the optic nerve or the brain causes the change, the color vision follows that damage. Color vision can also get worse with age, often because of cataracts.
utterances.captionText: Injuries and age both change color vision

utterances.spokenText: Most people with color vision deficiency manage everyday activities without major issues. Adaptive tools and simple strategies make daily life fully workable for them.
Most people with color vision deficiency live normal lives and face few real obstacles. They adapt easily and still handle ordinary tasks just like anyone else, day after day.
Simple tools and small adjustments make work, school, and home fully workable for them. Daily routines stay normal and independent every single day.

chapters.heading: Tools, limits, and everyday impact
chapters.summary: Notes there is no cure but special glasses and lenses can help, that the condition usually runs in families, and that most people do not have major problems with daily life.

utterances.spokenText: Complete color vision deficiency is rare. Most people with the condition still see some color rather than only black and white.
Because complete loss of color is uncommon, most people still experience hues and shades in daily life. They do not usually live in a fully grayscale world without color.
Seeing the world in only black and white is not the typical outcome for someone with this inherited condition. Total color vision loss remains the exception.

props.title: Inherited condition rarely removes all color

utterances.spokenText: Most affected individuals retain some color perception, even if distinguishing certain shades remains difficult. Total color blindness is therefore the exception rather than the rule.
Fifteen degrees above the horizon, sunlight travels a much longer path through the air. It passes through about three point eight six times more atmosphere than overhead sunlight.
That is nearly four times as much air for the light to cross. The extra distance comes from the shallow angle at which the rays enter the atmosphere.
Overhead, the Sun's light crosses just one unit of atmosphere. At fifteen degrees, that same beam stretches across roughly three point eight six units instead.
utterances.captionText: One unit overhead vs 3.86 units low.

utterances.spokenText: So a low Sun sends its light through far more air than a high Sun does. That longer path is the key difference at fifteen degrees elevation.
That longer path strips away much more blue light. The rays reaching your eyes near sunset are far richer in reds and yellows than overhead sunlight.
utterances.captionText: Sunset light carries more red and yellow.

props.title: Why sunset looks redder
steps: Blue scatters out of the beam
Reds and yellows reach your eyes

utterances.spokenText: High overhead, sunlight takes a short path through the air. It really stays bluer, while low-angle light arrives warmed by all that extra atmosphere above us.
utterances.captionText: Overhead light stays bluer; sunset light turns red.
